The goal of this notebook is to quantify the impact of large dams (see
[D12-dam-impact-presence.qmd]) on food web structure. To do so, we need to

- find descriptors of food web structure that can capture changes induced by
dams
- these descriptors can be based on presence-absence data or account for species
  biomass
- model the impact of dams on these descriptors
- investigate how the dam impact is mediated by species
- synthetise dam impacts and species-mediated effect on all descriptors
- investigate model residuals to see where the models fail

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(renv)
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
devtools::load_all()
nice_theme()
```

## Descriptors of food web structure

### List of descriptors

We use the visits of the presence models of D12 (target `dam_visit`) and
their observed food webs (D11), built from size classes: each fish species
is split into classes of body length that set its diet. For each web we
measure two types of metrics.

First, metrics based on presence-absence:

- **fish richness**: the number of fish species present
- **mean trophic level**: mean trophic level over the fish size classes
- **fish diet overlap**: the mean Jaccard similarity of the prey sets over pairs
  of fish size classes
- **trophic redundancy**: one minus the number of distinct trophic roles divided
  by the number of fish size classes, a role being a unique set of prey and
  predators.

Second, metrics based on biomass:

- **total biomass**: biomass summed over all individuals
- **mean trophic level**: the mean trophic level over the fish size classes,
weighted by their biomass
- **biomass-trophic level correlation**: the correlation between log biomass and
  trophic level of fish size classes.

### An illustrative example

To see what each metric measures, we compute them on a small invented web., with
The web as four species (A to D), split into two size classes for B, C and D,
and A has a single size class. D plays the role of a top predator, we look at
how the metrics respond to its loss.

```{r example-web}
metric_label <- c(
  fish_richness = "Fish richness",
  mean_trophic_level = "Mean trophic level",
  fish_diet_overlap = "Fish diet overlap",
  trophic_redundancy = "Trophic redundancy",
  log_biomass = "Total biomass (log)",
  biomass_trophic_level = "Mean trophic level (biomass)",
  biomass_pyramid = "Biomass-trophic level correlation"
)
example_resource <- c("biofilm", "detritus", "insect")
example_diet <- list(
  insect = c("biofilm", "detritus"),
  A_1 = c("biofilm", "insect"),
  B_1 = c("biofilm", "insect"),
  B_2 = c("insect", "A_1", "B_1"),
  C_1 = c("insect", "A_1", "B_1"),
  C_2 = c("insect", "B_2", "C_1"),
  D_1 = "insect",
  D_2 = c("B_2", "C_1", "C_2")
)
example_biomass <- c(
  A_1 = 900, B_1 = 1200, B_2 = 400, C_1 = 350, C_2 = 150, D_1 = 200, D_2 = 800
)
example_node <- c("biofilm", "detritus", names(example_diet))
example_full <- matrix(
  0L, length(example_node), length(example_node),
  dimnames = list(example_node, example_node)
)
for (predator in names(example_diet)) {
  example_full[example_diet[[predator]], predator] <- 1L
}
example_kept <- !startsWith(example_node, "D_")
example_web <- list(
  `Full web` = example_full,
  `Without species D` = example_full[example_kept, example_kept]
)
example_metric <- purrr::map_dfr(
  example_web, measure_web, resource = example_resource,
  biomass = example_biomass, .id = "web"
)
```

Here are the web we consider for our illustrative exercise.

```{r example-web-plot}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

example_x <- c(
  biofilm = 1, detritus = 3, insect = 2.3, A_1 = 0.9, B_1 = 1.8, B_2 = 1.3,
  C_1 = 2.2, C_2 = 1.75, D_1 = 3.3, D_2 = 2.9
)
example_position <- purrr::imap_dfr(example_web, \(foodweb, web) tibble(
  web, node = colnames(foodweb),
  level = compute_prey_averaged_trophic_level(
    igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(foodweb), example_resource
  ),
  x = example_x[node]
))
example_link <- purrr::imap_dfr(example_web, \(foodweb, web) {
  link <- which(foodweb > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
  tibble(web, prey = rownames(foodweb)[link[, 1]], predator = colnames(foodweb)[link[, 2]])
}) |>
  left_join(example_position, by = c("web", "prey" = "node")) |>
  left_join(example_position, by = c("web", "predator" = "node"), suffix = c("", "_end"))
example_fish <- example_position |>
  filter(!node %in% example_resource) |>

    biomass = example_biomass[node],
    species = if_else(startsWith(node, "D_"), "Species D", "Species A to C"),
    label = sub("_", "", node)
  )
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = example_link, aes(x, level, xend = x_end, yend = level_end),
    color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(example_position, node %in% example_resource), aes(x, level),
    shape = 15, size = 3, color = "grey45"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = filter(example_position, node %in% example_resource),
    aes(x, level, label = node), nudge_y = -0.22, size = 3.3, color = "grey20"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = example_fish, aes(x, level, size = biomass, fill = species),
    shape = 21, color = "white", stroke = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = example_fish, aes(x, level, label = label),
    nudge_x = 0.2, nudge_y = 0.17, size = 3.3, color = "grey20"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~web) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 13, breaks = c(200, 500, 1000)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Species A to C` = "#2166AC", `Species D` = "#B2182B")) +
  scale_x_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL, expand = expansion(mult = 0.1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5, limits = c(0.7, 5)) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5)),
    size = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = "grey60"))
  ) +
  labs(y = "Trophic level", size = "Biomass (g)", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

And here are the values of the selected metrics for the two webs.

```{r example-web-metrics}
example_metric |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-web, names_to = "metric") |>
  filter(metric %in% names(metric_label)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = web) |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric_label[metric], metric_label)) |>
  arrange(metric) |>
  rename(Metric = metric) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

Without D, species richness and biomass drops. The food web also becomes
simpler, which is capture by a lower mean trophic level and higher trophic
redundancy. Finally, more of the biomass is at the base of the web, which is
captured by the decrease of the biomass-trophic level correlation, which goes to
-1.

### Metrics observed in reconsutructred food webs

We exclude the 28 webs in which a fish size class has no prey, as its trophic
level would then be that of a basal resource.

```{r webs}
web <- tar_read(dam_foodweb)
```

We first plot the distribution of the metrics over the webs of the visits.

```{r web-distribution}

#| fig-height: 5

web |>

  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric_label[metric], metric_label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    # One bin per value for the counts (richness), 30 bins otherwise.
    binwidth = \(x) if (all(x == round(x))) 1 else diff(range(x)) / 30,
    fill = "#2166AC", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2, na.rm = TRUE

```

And the Spearman correlation between the metrics over the webs.

To see how the metrics play together, we also run a principal component analysis
on the scaled metrics of the visits where all of them are defined.

```{r web-pca}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

web_pca <- tar_read(structure_pca)
pca_variance <- round(100 * summary(web_pca)$importance["Proportion of Variance", ])
pca_axis <- paste0(names(pca_variance), " (", pca_variance, "%)")
# Correlation of each metric with the axes.
pca_correlation <- as_tibble(t(t(web_pca$rotation) * web_pca$sdev), rownames = "metric") |>
  mutate(metric = metric_label[metric])
arrow_length <- 3 # Stretches the correlations to the range of the visits.
ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = as_tibble(web_pca$x), aes(PC1 / sd(PC1), PC2 / sd(PC2)),
    color = "grey75", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_segment(
    data = pca_correlation,
    aes(0, 0, xend = arrow_length * PC1, yend = arrow_length * PC2),
    color = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.7, arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"))
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = pca_correlation,
    aes(arrow_length * PC1, arrow_length * PC2, label = metric),
    size = 3.5, color = "grey20", seed = 1, min.segment.length = Inf,
    bg.color = "white", bg.r = 0.15
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = pca_axis[1], y = pca_axis[2])
```

Loading of each metric with the first two axes.

```{r web-pca-table}
pca_correlation |>
  select(Metric = metric, PC1, PC2) |>
  rename_with(\(x) pca_axis[match(x, names(pca_variance))], c(PC1, PC2)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r web-pca-composition}
species_presence <- tar_read(species_presence)
pca_score <- scale(predict(web_pca, web)[, c("PC1", "PC2")])
axis_name <- c(PC1 = "PC1", PC2 = "PC2")
complete_visit <- complete.cases(pca_score)
composition_presence <- species_presence[complete_visit, ]
```

We investigate also how species presence influence PCA axis. For each axis, we
keep the four species with the highest and the four with the lowest correlation.

```{r web-pca-species}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5

frequent_presence <- composition_presence[, colSums(composition_presence) >= 100]
purrr::map_dfr(names(axis_name), \(axis) tibble(
  label = axis_name[axis],
  species = colnames(frequent_presence),
  correlation = apply(frequent_presence, 2, \(x) cor(x, pca_score[complete_visit, axis]))
)) |>
  (\(x) bind_rows(
    slice_max(x, correlation, n = 4, by = label),
    slice_min(x, correlation, n = 4, by = label)
  ))() |>
  mutate(species = reorder(paste(species, label, sep = "___"), correlation)) |>
  ggplot(aes(correlation, species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = correlation, yend = species), color = "#2166AC", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(color = "#2166AC", size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = \(x) sub("___.*", "", x)) +
  facet_wrap(~label, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Correlation with the presence of the species", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"))
```

Map of mean score of each site on the two CPA axes, over its visits.

```{r web-pca-map}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5

basin_kept <- tar_read(basin) |>
  filter(district %in% tar_read(params)$district_kept)
site_axis <- web |>
  mutate(PC1 = pca_score[, "PC1"], PC2 = pca_score[, "PC2"]) |>
  filter(complete_visit) |>
  mutate(PC1 = mean(PC1), PC2 = mean(PC2), .by = sandre_code) |>
  distinct(sandre_code, .keep_all = TRUE)
site_location <- visit_coordinates(site_axis) * 1000
site_axis |>
  transmute(x = site_location[, 1], y = site_location[, 2], PC1, PC2) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(PC1, PC2), names_to = "axis", values_to = "score") |>
  mutate(axis = axis_name[axis]) |>
  arrange(abs(score)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 2154), fill = NA, color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(aes(x, y, color = score), size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~axis) +
  scale_color_distiller(
    palette = "PuOr", direction = 1, limits = c(-2.5, 2.5),
    oob = scales::squish, name = "Mean score"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

No single axis sums up all the food web structure. Yet, the first two axes
explain together more than half of it. 

**PC1.** PC1 is about how simple the web is. Low
scores are rich webs holding much biomass, high in the web; high scores are webs
with few species, little biomass, low in the web, and fish that are alike (high
diet overlap and trophic redundancy). Low scores are found in webs with the eel,
the pike or the wels catfish; we call it the simplicity axis. 

**PC2.** PC2 opposes species-poor webs where the biomass is concentrated high in
the web, often with brown trout, to species-rich webs that are less top-heavy,
with more biomass in species feeding low in the web. We call it the richness to
top-heaviness gradient. It could indicate polluted water, as it is strongly
correlated with the presence of *Rutilus rutilus* which is a species known to
tolerate polluted water, and take strong values in estuaries.

## Model dam impacts on food web structure

We model the impacts of dams on food web descriptors using the model structure
from [presence models (see notebook D12)](D12-dam-impact-presence.qmd).
We use Gaussian distribution except for fish richness for which we use a Poisson
distribution (because it seems *a propos*). In addition of the descriptors
listed above, we also model the scores of the two PCA axes.

```{r structure-models}
structure_setting <- tar_read(structure_setting)
structure_effect <- purrr::map2_dfr(
  tar_read(structure_model), structure_setting$richness,
  \(model, richness) model$summary.fixed |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
    transmute(
      metric = model$metric, richness, term,
      mean, lower = `0.045quant`, upper = `0.955quant`
    )
) |>
  filter(metric %in% names(metric_label)) |>
  left_join(
    web |>
      summarise(across(all_of(names(metric_label)), \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
      tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "metric", values_to = "sd"),
    by = "metric"
  ) |>
  # Gaussian metrics on the sd scale, to compare them; richness stays on the
  # log scale.
  mutate(
    across(c(mean, lower, upper), \(x) if_else(metric == "fish_richness", x, x / sd)),
    control = if_else(richness, "with richness", "without richness")
  )
```

```{r structure-dam-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

structure_label <- c(
  metric_label,
  PC1 = "PC1", PC2 = "PC2"
)
structure_axis_setting <- tar_read(structure_axis_setting)
axis_effect <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(structure_axis_setting)), \(i) {
  dam <- tar_read(structure_axis_model)[[i]]$summary.fixed["accumulation", ]
  tibble(
    metric = structure_axis_setting$axis[i],
    control = if_else(structure_axis_setting$richness[i], "with richness", "without richness"),
    mean = dam$mean, lower = dam$`0.045quant`, upper = dam$`0.955quant`
  )
})
structure_effect |>
  filter(term == "accumulation") |>
  bind_rows(axis_effect) |>
  mutate(metric = factor(structure_label[metric], rev(structure_label))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, metric, color = control)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
    position = position_dodge(0.5), size = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`without richness` = "grey40", `with richness` = "#2166AC")) +
  labs(x = "Effect of log(1 + dams)", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Dams make food web simpler: less species, less biomass, especially at the top,
more redundant species. This result is supported by individual descriptors on
the first PCA axis. However, dams show no credible effect PC2 because this axis
combine two descriptors on which dams act in opposition: fish richness and mean
trophic level. This mean that this joint variation are not impacted by dams;
they may be for example caused by other stressors (nutrients), or unobserved
environmental driver.

## How species mediate dam effect on food web structure

We now ask which species mediate the dam effect on food web structure. We
summarise the structure with PC1 for simplicity. We do this in 3 steps.

1. **Species contribution to structure.** Each fish species of each web is
   removed in turn (all its size classes), and PC1 is computed again on the
   remaining web (webs with at least 3 fish species). We note $r_s$ the change
   of PC1 when species $s$ is removed, in standard deviations of PC1, averaged
   over the visits of each site and then over the sites.
2. **Dam impact on species presence.** With the presence models of D12, one more
unit of $\log(1 + \text{dams})$ changes the presence probability of species $s$ by
   $\beta_s \overline{p_s (1 - p_s)}$, with $\beta_s$ its dam effect on the
   logit scale and $p_s$ its fitted presence probability, averaged over the
   visits.
3. **Combining the two.** The contribution of species $s$ to the dam effect on
   PC1 is its change of presence times the change of PC1 that its presence
   brings, and the expected dam effect is the sum over the species:
$$
\Delta = \sum_s \beta_s \, \overline{p_s (1 - p_s)} \, (-r_s).
$$

The uncertainty of $\beta_s$ and $r_s$ is propagated by drawing both. To know
whether dams affect the species that matter more for the structure, we compare
$\Delta$ with a null model where the dam effects $\beta_s$ are shuffled among
the species: the loss is as large, but falls on random species.

```{r species-mediation}
presence_model <- tar_read(presence_model)
decomposition <- tar_read(structure_decomposition)
permutation <- tar_read(structure_permutation)
species_step <- c(
  importance = "Contribution to PC1",
  presence = "Dam impact on presence",
  contribution = "Dam effect mediated by the species"
)
species_mediation <- decomposition$species |>
  filter(metric == "PC1") |>
  left_join(select(filter(tar_read(species_removal_effect), metric == "PC1"), species, importance = mean,
                   importance_lower = lower, importance_upper = upper), by = "species")
```

We plot the dam effect on PC1 estimated by the model, predicted from the loss of
species to dam, and predicted using the same loss but randomised among species,
without and at equal richness. To predict the effect at equal richness, the
change of PC1 when a species is removed is corrected by the change expected from
having one species fewer, that is the effect of log richness in the model of PC1
with richness times the change of log richness when the species is removed.

```{r species-mediation-total}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.8

estimate_level <- c(
  "Estimated by the model", "Predicted from species loss", "Null (shuffled dam effects)"
)
metric_control <- c(PC1 = "without richness", PC1_richness = "with richness")
bind_rows(
  axis_effect |>
    filter(metric == "PC1") |>
    transmute(estimate = estimate_level[1], control, mean, lower, upper),
  bind_rows(
    decomposition$draw |> mutate(estimate = estimate_level[2]),
    permutation |> mutate(estimate = estimate_level[3])
  ) |>
    summarise(
      mean = mean(change), lower = quantile(change, 0.045), upper = quantile(change, 0.955),
      .by = c(metric, estimate)
    ) |>
    transmute(estimate, control = metric_control[metric], mean, lower, upper)
) |>
  mutate(estimate = factor(estimate, rev(estimate_level))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, estimate, color = control)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper),
    position = position_dodge(0.5), size = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`without richness` = "grey40", `with richness` = "#2166AC")) +
  labs(x = "Dam effect on PC1 (sd of PC1 per unit of log(1 + dams))", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Next we plot the decomposition of the predicted effect from species loss at the
species level. We keep the species with the stronger mediated effect.

```{r species-mediation-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6

bind_rows(
  species_mediation |> transmute(species, step = "importance", mean = importance, lower = importance_lower, upper = importance_upper),
  species_mediation |> transmute(species, step = "presence", mean = presence, lower = presence_lower, upper = presence_upper),
  species_mediation |> transmute(species, step = "contribution", mean = contribution, lower, upper)
) |>
  semi_join(slice_max(species_mediation, abs(contribution), n = 15), by = "species") |>
  mutate(
    step = factor(species_step[step], species_step),
    species = factor(species, arrange(species_mediation, contribution)$species)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, species)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), size = 0.3, color = "#2166AC") +
  facet_wrap(~step, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"))
```

Species have varied influence on food web structure. Piscivorous are the most
important species. Dam has also varied impact on species. Anadromous species, or
brackish species are the most affects. Overall this make the eel, which is a
large piscivorous species and anadromous, the main mediating species of the dam
impact.
